To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the 2008 revision of the Declaration of Helsinki (DOH) is the first version of the DOH to contain a preponderance of "must" over "should" prescriptors, (b) this inversion is significant because the DOH is widely regarded as'soft law', and (c) the significance of the inversion is that it signals that the DOH is intended to set out categorical, perfect and obligatory requirements

1) the Declaration is best understood as a form of soft law, which has the status of an ethical guideline, not as a binding instrument of international law; 2) "should" is a weaker term than "must" in the sense of categorical requirements, and the 2008 version is more stringent than the 2000 version in that respect; 3) the 2000 and 2008 versions are equally stringent in their requirements for the protection of research participants;

(1) The Declaration of Helsinki (2000 version) contains 33 uses of "must" and 57 uses of "should"; (2) The 2000 draft contained 33 uses of must and 58 uses of "should" (3) The 2008 final draft contained 33 "must" and just 2 "should"; (4) In 2000 "must" was more common in the sections dealing with informed consent and research involving vulnerable groups.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the terms "must" and "should" should be understood in a legal context.
the interpretation of a document that is widely viewed as the authoritative ethical code for medical research, and that is often used in legislative and jurisdiction contexts.
the way in which obligations are expressed in ethical codes, and the implications of this for their interpretation and application.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the 2008 version of the Declaration of Helsinki contains a mixture of perfect and imperfect obligations and categorical and hypothetical requirements, and that these should be interpreted as aspirational and not binding.
the Declaration sets out a series of strong categorical requirements.
the 2008 Declaration of Helsinki is a soft law instrument which, when interpreted in the light of the distinction between "should" and'must', sets out a number of strong categorical obligations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 2008 Declaration of Helsinki is a more categorical statement of ethical requirements than its 2000 predecessor, but it is also more ambiguous and open to different readings.
the "should"/"must" distinction in the Declaration of Helsinki is best understood as an expression of the strength of the ethical requirements which it sets out.
the Declaration's "should" statements are intended to be categorical obligations; whereas its "must" statements are aspirational.
The main takeaway from our work is that
should" and must" should not be regarded as interchangeable.
the distinction between "should" and must" is not a simple one, and that it has implications for the interpretation of the Declaration of Helsinki.
the Declaration of Helsinki is a document of great importance to the conduct and regulation of biomedical research. But its interpretation and implementation are complex and contested.
